text:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, nephew of the deceased, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, I am sorry to keep you up. Sit wherever you are comfortable. You are the master's nephew?

FÉLIX: His brother's son. Jules's boy. You will want to know whether I was fond of him, and I will save you the trouble. When he was not insulting me, yes, I was.

MATTHEY: Tell me about this evening, from dinner.

FÉLIX: Dinner was the usual business. Uncle keeps a custom every year. When the temple strikes nine, everyone at the table must take out his watch, and he tells you what is wrong with it. Aunt Odile thinks it is a sort of party game. It was not a game to him. Mine showed twenty minutes to nine when the bell struck nine, and he made a scene about it in front of everybody. He said my father's watch was an insult to the trade.

MATTHEY: Your father's watch?

FÉLIX: The silver one. It was his, and I have carried it since he died. I have never let anyone regulate it. Not my uncle, though he asked me every Christmas, and he asked me at dinner too, in front of the Doctor and the Girard fellow. I did not give it to him.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

FÉLIX: I went up to the library and stayed there. I am not proud of it. I had brandy, alone, and I had more than I should. I was frightened, Inspector, and I do not know of what. Of Uncle, I suppose. Of the bills.

MATTHEY: Take your time.

FÉLIX: When the temple struck ten my watch showed twenty to ten. I know because I looked at it. I look at it every time I am frightened, which is often lately.

MATTHEY: Go on.

FÉLIX: At a quarter past ten by my watch someone went quickly up the stairs, past the library door. Quickly, I would say. I did not see who. The door was shut. I have said that and I will say it again, so that you do not have to write it twice.

MATTHEY: Yes. Go on.

FÉLIX: At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. My aunt's piano was playing downstairs when it came. Then Uncle's repeater. Ten slow deep notes, I counted those. Then some doubled notes, for the quarters, and then quick high ones, which I did not count. I would know that repeater in my sleep. He made it for the new century. He told everyone so, and he made sure everyone heard about the four years of it.

MATTHEY: You knew what it meant to him.

FÉLIX: Everyone knew. It was the only thing he loved as much as he loved being right.

MATTHEY: And then?

FÉLIX: At twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch someone came quickly down the stairs. The same as before, quick, and the door was shut. I did not see who.

MATTHEY: Monsieur Girard. When did he come to you?

FÉLIX: Bastien came into the library at thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch. We sat together there until the temple struck eleven. He did not say much. He never says much when he is about to talk about money. I owe him some of it. He knows the sum better than I do.

MATTHEY: You have nothing more to tell me about the stairs?

FÉLIX: Nothing. I have told you all of it, and I have told you the truth, which is more than I have told my own mother.

MATTHEY: Thank you. You have been very clear.

FÉLIX: Clear. Yes. That is what frightens me, Inspector. I was one floor below the atelier with a bottle and a dead man's watch in my pocket, and I am the heir. You can see how it looks.

MATTHEY: I can see that you are tired, Monsieur. We will speak again.
